method: S1 is the open RACGP AJGP case study of MARCH 2026 -- six months old -- fetched and checked verbatim (18 claims, 4 of them doses). A1 is AMH across two topics, paraphrased, no passage reproduced and no source_text stored (21 claims, 4 doses). The ORAL DOSES ARE QUOTED from the open source: AMH's table names first and alternative agents by organism and site but gives no milligrams, while S1 gives terbinafine 250 mg daily and itraconazole 100 mg daily. The two sources differ on DIAGNOSTIC METHOD -- A1 says microscopy and culture, S1 says PCR is preferred where available and faster and more sensitive -- and both are stated. S1 is a single case report and its generalisable content is separated in the guideline from what happened to its one patient.

claims.claim: S1 lists clinical findings suggestive of fungal infection as skin and/or hair and nail involvement and pruritus, with risk factors of public changerooms, pets, overseas travel and immunosuppression, while findings not suggestive include systemic symptoms, constitutional symptoms, pain, and triggers such as photosensitivity, new medication or new topical exposures
claims.source_text: Clinical findings suggestive of fungal infection - Skin and/or hair and nail involvement - Pruritus - Risk factors: public changerooms, pets, overseas travel, immunosuppression Clinical findings not suggestive of fungal infection - Systemic symptoms - Constitutional symptoms - Pain - Triggers: photosensitivity, new medication, new topical exposures

claims.claim: S1 states that atypical presentation known as tinea incognito is due to partial treatment and/or corticosteroid use, and that isolated tinea unguium requires careful exclusion of other more sinister conditions such as squamous cell carcinoma or nail bed melanoma
claims.source_text: Atypical presentation ('tinea incognito') - due to partial treatment and/or corticosteroid use - Isolated tinea unguium - requires careful exclusion of other more sinister conditions (ie squamous cell carcinoma or nail bed melanoma)

claims.claim: S1 notes that the body site affected influences treatment route and duration, that regular medications may interact with future potential therapy, and that neonates and infants require closer monitoring with or without paediatric dermatologist opinion when given oral treatment
claims.source_text: Body site affected - influences treatment route and duration - Regular medications - may interact with future potential therapy - Neonates and infants - require more close monitoring +/- paediatric dermatologist opinion with oral treatment

claims.claim: Dermatophyte infections are transmitted through direct skin contact with an infected person or animal, or indirectly through exposure to fungal spores, and tinea is a clinical diagnosis with confirmation from tissue microscopy, culture and polymerase chain reaction
claims.source_text: Dermatophyte infections are transmitted through direct skin contact with an infected person or animal, or indirectly through exposure to fungal spores. 1 Tinea infection is a clinical diagnosis with confirmation from tissue microscopy, culture and polymerase chain reaction (PCR).

claims.claim: S1 advises that samples should be collected prior to treatment initiation and of sufficient quantity to reduce false-negative results, and that skin scrapings should ideally be taken from a lesion that has not been recently treated with a topical antifungal agent
claims.source_text: Samples should be collected prior to treatment initiation and of sufficient quantity to reduce false-negative results. 2 Skin scrapings should ideally be taken from a lesion that has not been recently treated with a topical antifungal agent.

claims.claim: S1 advises a scalpel at a blunt angle to collect skin scrapings, nail samples including clippings and scrapings of subungual debris using a scalpel or curette, and a hair sample removed using tweezers to include the root with surrounding skin scrapings, with yellow-top specimen containers used for all sample sites
claims.source_text: A scalpel at a blunt angle to the skin can be used to collect an adequate sample. 2 Nail samples include clippings and scrapings of subungual debris using a scalpel or curette. A hair sample can be removed using tweezers to include the root in conjunction with surrounding skin scrapings. 2 Yellow-top specimen containers are used for all sample sites, accompanied by pathology requests with appropriate labelling of specimen type and location.

claims.claim: S1 states that PCR testing is available in some Australian laboratories and preferred because of its faster turnaround and superior sensitivity and specificity compared with microscopy and culture, and that if PCR is not accessible fungal microscopy and culture is inexpensive and acceptable though culture can take up to 6 weeks
claims.source_text: PCR testing is available in some Australian laboratories and preferred because of its faster turnaround and superior sensitivity and specificity when compared with microscopy and culture (MCS). 3 If PCR is not accessible, fungal MCS is inexpensive and acceptable, though culture can take up to 6 weeks.

claims.claim: Trichophyton rubrum is the leading cause of tinea worldwide, while other species such as Microsporum canis, T. mentagrophytes and T. verrucosum may be associated with zoonotic exposure through pets such as cats and dogs or other animals such as cows and horses
claims.source_text: Trichophyton rubrum is the leading cause of tinea worldwide. 1,5 Other species, such as Microsporum canis, T. mentagrophytes and T. verrucosum, may be associated with zoonotic exposure through pets (cats, dogs) or other animals (cows, horses).

claims.claim: S1 states that localised mild skin infections can be treated with topical terbinafine or azoles, and that oral therapies are indicated for tinea capitis, widespread infection, immunocompromised status, failed response to topical treatment, or involvement of the palms, soles or nails
claims.source_text: Localised mild skin infections can be treated with topical therapies including terbinafine or azoles. 6 Oral therapies are indicated for tinea capitis, widespread infection, immunocompromised status, failed response to topical treatment or when there is involvement of the palms, soles or nails.

claims.claim: S1 gives oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 2 weeks as the preferred regimen with longer courses indicated when there is nail or scalp involvement, and itraconazole 100 mg daily for 2 to 4 weeks as an oral alternative
claims.source_text: Oral terbinafine 250 mg daily for 2 weeks is the preferred regimen, with longer courses indicated when there is nail or scalp involvement. … Itraconazole 100 mg daily for 2-4 weeks is an oral alternative to terbinafine.

claims.claim: S1 states terbinafine is generally well tolerated with a small risk of gastrointestinal side effects and transient liver enzyme elevation, with rare complications including hepatitis, photosensitivity, pancytopenia, cutaneous lupus and Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis
claims.source_text: Terbinafine is generally well tolerated with a small risk of gastrointestinal side effects and transient liver enzyme elevation. Rare complications include hepatitis, photosensitivity, pancytopenia, cutaneous lupus and Stevens-Johnson Syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis.

claims.claim: S1 states that dose adjustment of terbinafine is indicated in renal impairment and that monitoring of liver function and full blood count is recommended with courses longer than 6 weeks duration
claims.source_text: Dose adjustment is indicated in renal impairment. Monitoring of liver function and full blood count is recommended with courses longer than 6 weeks duration.

claims.claim: S1 states that ketoconazole or selenium sulphide shampoo can be used as a treatment adjunct for tinea capitis
claims.source_text: Ketoconazole or selenium sulphide shampoo can be used as a treatment adjunct for tinea capitis.

claims.claim: S1 states that if there is good compliance and appropriate route of therapy yet inadequate treatment response, alternative diagnoses as well as terbinafine-resistant species should be considered, and that high rates of terbinafine-resistant T. interdigitale species have been reported in India, Europe and more recently Australia
claims.source_text: If there is good compliance and appropriate route of therapy, yet inadequate treatment response, alternative diagnoses as well as terbinafine-resistant species should be considered. High rates of terbinafine-resistant T. interdigitale species have been reported in India, Europe and, more recently, Australia.

claims.claim: S1 states that corticosteroid-modified tinea, known as tinea incognito, masks the classical clinical presentation and can delay diagnosis, and that topical steroids have an immunosuppressive effect that can compromise the efficacy of antifungal treatment
claims.source_text: Corticosteroid-modified tinea, 'tinea incognito', masks the classical clinical presentation and can delay diagnosis. Topical steroids have an immunosuppressive effect that can compromise the efficacy of antifungal treatment.

claims.claim: S1 states the dermatophyte infects the stratum corneum only with an incubation period of 1 to 3 weeks, that fungal spores shed from the skin persist in warm moist environments, and that cases of recurrent tinea should be evaluated for any potential reservoir of dermatophytes, commonly toenails
claims.source_text: The dermatophyte infects the stratum corneum only with an incubation period of 1-3 weeks. 1 Fungal spores shed from the skin persist in warm, moist environments. … Cases of recurrent tinea should be evaluated for any potential reservoir of dermatophytes, commonly toenails.

claims.claim: S1 advises prevention measures including good personal hygiene and avoidance of routes of spread such as sharing combs, bedding, towels or clothing, and specifically for tinea pedis drying between toe web spaces and wearing thongs in public showers and changerooms
claims.source_text: Measures to prevent initial or recurrent infection include good personal hygiene and avoidance of routes of spread, such as sharing of combs, bedding, towels or clothing. Specifically for tinea pedis, drying between toe web spaces and wearing thongs in public showers/changerooms is important.

claims.claim: In S1's case both skin scraping and nail clipping returned positive for T. rubrum on PCR but only the nail clipping showed fungal filaments on microscopy, demonstrating the rapid and superior sensitivity of PCR, and the patient was continued on oral terbinafine to complete a total 3-month course given nail involvement
claims.source_text: Both samples returned positive for T. rubrum on PCR, but only the nail clipping showed fungal filaments on microscopy, demonstrating the rapid and superior sensitivity of PCR. … Given his good clinical response but presence of nail involvement, he was continued on oral terbinafine to complete a total 3-month course.

claims.claim: Tinea is a superficial fungal infection of the skin, hair or nails caused by dermatophytes, classified by the area affected as tinea capitis for scalp and hair, tinea corporis or ringworm for trunk or limbs, tinea cruris for groin, tinea pedis or athlete's foot for the foot, and tinea unguium for the nail
